subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Asia
subtitle: Reading passages and comprehension questions about Asia as a world region.
description: Five reading passages for middle school geography students. The passages test understanding of Asia's subregions, physical geography, monsoons, population patterns, resources, trade, hazards, and sustainability.

data.sourcePassage: Asia is the largest and most populated continent on Earth. It stretches from cold Arctic areas in the north to tropical islands near the Equator, and from Western Asia near Europe and Africa to East Asia facing the Pacific Ocean. Geographers often divide Asia into subregions such as East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, Western Asia, and North Asia. These subregions help students see patterns, but the borders are not always simple. Some countries connect to more than one region historically, culturally, or physically. Turkey and Russia are examples of countries often linked to both Asia and Europe. Studying Asia means looking for contrasts: wet and dry climates, crowded river valleys and sparse deserts, ancient trade routes and modern shipping networks, wealthy technology hubs and rural farming communities.

data.sourcePassage: Asia has some of Earth's most dramatic physical features. The Himalaya Mountains are the world's highest mountain range, and the Tibetan Plateau north of them helps feed major rivers. Rivers such as the Yangtze, Yellow, Ganges, Indus, Mekong, Tigris, and Euphrates have supported farms, towns, cities, transport, and early civilizations. River valleys and deltas often attract large populations because they provide water, fertile soil, fish, and routes for movement. However, the same places can face flood risk. Other environments, such as the Gobi Desert, Arabian Desert, high mountains, and cold Siberian plains, usually have lower population density because farming, travel, and construction are harder. Physical geography does not control everything people do, but it strongly shapes opportunities and challenges.

data.sourcePassage: The monsoon is one of Asia's most important climate patterns. In South Asia, summer winds bring moist air from the Indian Ocean, causing heavy rainfall across places such as India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and parts of Pakistan and Sri Lanka. The monsoon supports farming by bringing water for crops such as rice, tea, and cotton. It also refills rivers, reservoirs, and groundwater and can support hydropower. At the same time, the monsoon can be dangerous. Very heavy rain may cause flooding, landslides, damaged roads, crop loss, and disease if sanitation systems are overwhelmed. Too little rain can cause drought and crop failure. Communities adapt with flood warnings, raised homes, embankments, drainage systems, water storage, and crop calendars that match the rainy season.

data.sourcePassage: Asia is home to more than half of the world's people, but population is not spread evenly. High population density often occurs near fertile river valleys, reliable water supplies, coastal trade routes, productive farmland, historic cities, and job centers. Examples include the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, eastern China, Japan's coastal urban belt, Java, and the Manila region. Lower population density is more common in deserts, high mountains, dense forests, very cold regions, and places with limited transport. Many Asian cities have grown rapidly through urbanization. People may migrate from rural areas to cities for jobs, schools, health care, safety, or family connections. Migration can bring opportunities, but it can also create pressure on housing, transport, water, electricity, and waste systems.

data.sourcePassage: Asia has many important resources, but they are unevenly distributed. Western Asia and parts of Central Asia and Russia have large oil and natural gas reserves. South, East, and Southeast Asia have major rice-growing areas, fisheries, and manufacturing regions. East Asian coastal cities are important in global supply chains for electronics, cars, ships, and consumer goods. Central Asia has energy, minerals, cotton-growing areas, and livestock, but its landlocked location makes transport routes especially important. Sustainability challenges include water scarcity, pollution, overused groundwater, fossil fuel dependence, deforestation, overfishing, and fast-growing cities. Sustainable solutions include renewable energy, cleaner public transportation, water conservation, reforestation, floodplain planning, waste management, and protecting wetlands, coral reefs, and forests.

questions.question: Why are transport routes especially important for Central Asia?
questions.modelAnswer: Much of Central Asia is landlocked, so goods must move through land routes, railways, roads, and connections to other regions.

questions.question: Give one sustainable solution named in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include renewable energy, cleaner public transportation, water conservation, reforestation, floodplain planning, waste management, or ecosystem protection.

questions.question: Why can depending heavily on one resource be risky for a region?
questions.modelAnswer: If prices change, demand falls, or environmental costs rise, a region that depends on one resource may lose income and jobs.
